newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Talks on new Albanian government, more towns fall.
newsitem.headline: Talks on new Albanian government, more towns fall.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha resumed talks with political party leaders on Tuesday on a new national unity government as rebels tightened their grip on the south of the country.
Rebels took control of several more major towns on Monday to move the insurgency sparked by the collapse of pyramid savings schemes to within 85 km (55 miles) of the capital Tirana in the north.

Late on Monday Italy brokered a deal with rebel leaders in Vlore, the focal point of the rebellion, with a declaration backing a weekend call for a new government and pledging to seek the surrender of weapons seized from army depots.

It was unclear, however, whether other rebel-held towns would follow Vlore's example. The southern port has organised itself under a rebel council headed by a former army general, while insurgents in some other towns appear to be operating without leaders.

In Tirana, talks on forming a new all-party government were due to resume at midday after participants agreed on Monday to split cabinet posts evenly between the ruling Democratic Party and the opposition.

However the two sides were deadlocked on who gets the key portfolios. Political sources said both Berisha and the ex-communist Socialists, the main opposition party, were insisting on holding the Interior Ministry.
The ministry is responsible among other things for local councils and the police, which will both play a key role in organising new elections, due to be held by June.

Last year's elections, which gave Berisha 122 seats in the 140-member parliament, were boycotted by the opposition amid allegations of intimidation and vote-rigging, and were widely criticised by international observers.
The sources said the Socialists were also insisting on the release of their leader Fatos Nano, in jail after being convicted on corruption charges the party says were politically inspired.
The latest areas to fall into rebel hands included the ancient town of Berat, near Kucove, site of one of two big Albanian air force bases, and Permet, a remote mountain town.

Representatives of rebels controlling Vlore, site of some of Albania's fiercest rioting, signed a declaration seeking quick implementation of the weekend accord signed by Berisha and opposition parties.
The deal calls for an all-party government, elections by June and an amnesty for anyone handing in arms within a week.

"The committee...undertook to favour the immediate handing back of weapons in the hands of the citizens of Vlore and to ensure public order and progessively restore normal administration to the town," the declaration said.

The statement was signed on an Italian warship in the Adriatic after talks with Italy's ambassador to Tirana. Italy has been asked by Albania to underwrite the weekend agreement between Berisha and the parties on securing a political solution.
Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini was reported on Tuesday to have cancelled a trip to India so that he can remain in Italy to follow the Albanian crisis.
In Washington, the U.S. State Department welcomed the peace efforts and called on the rebels in the south to lay down their arms.

The Council of Europe, which safeguards democracy and human rights, also urged Albanians to hand back their weapons without delay "so as to allow the rule of law to prevail and democracy to function".
At least 40 people have died in the latest wave of disturbances over the past 10 days.
